title: The team assumes it needs the largest model
situation: A team needs concise summaries and reliable categories within a strict latency and token-cost budget. It proposes the largest available model before testing representative inputs.
meaning: The requirement is measured task quality under constraints. Model size is a candidate characteristic, not an acceptance criterion.
evidence: Compare supported candidates on the same held-out cases, including difficult inputs and critical cohorts. Check capability, context/output limits, quality, latency, and cost.
rule: Choose by representative workload fit; public benchmark rank or model size alone is insufficient.

title: Answers need current private facts
situation: An assistant explains policies clearly but cannot answer questions about recently changed internal rules. The team proposes fine-tuning to make every future answer current.
meaning: The missing requirement is access to fresh, permitted evidence. Changing weights alone does not supply a live authoritative source.
evidence: Check source freshness, caller entitlement, whether the required fact reaches context, and whether citations support the answer.
rule: Private/current/attributable knowledge → evaluate RAG. RAG and customization can combine when their requirements differ.

title: Format and task rules are unclear
situation: Equivalent inputs receive different categories and inconsistent output shapes. The team has not defined category boundaries, supplied examples, or validated the business meaning of the result.
meaning: Clarify what a correct answer means before treating the behavior as a model-capability or training defect.
evidence: Review task definitions, governing instructions, representative examples, supported output constraints, and schema plus business assertions.
rule: Task/format gaps → start with prompting and supported structured output. Valid JSON or low temperature is not proof of a correct decision.

title: Stable behavior still fails clear prompts
situation: The team has clear task rules, correct evidence, and evaluated prompt examples. A suitable baseline still misses a required stable style or classification behavior across representative cases.
meaning: Supported customization may fit an evaluated behavior gap. This differs from missing current evidence or ambiguous instructions.
evidence: Check supervision quality, held-out improvement, safety/cohort regressions, lifecycle cost, and compatibility with the intended deployment.
rule: Consider supported customization only for the measured gap; evaluate it against prompting/RAG baselines and verify deployment support.

title: Fluent output hides an invalid business action
situation: An assistant proposes a well-formed refund request for an account outside the caller’s scope. The team proposes a larger model instead of enforcing the business preconditions.
meaning: Language quality does not establish authorization or valid transaction semantics. Identify the control requirement independently of model choice.
evidence: Inspect the effective caller, permitted record/action scope, actual tool arguments, approval requirements, and authoritative business outcome.
rule: Enforce deterministic authorization and action checks. A fluent answer or valid JSON is not a completed, permitted business action.

title: Domain adaptation is mistaken for live knowledge
situation: A domain-adapted model still gives an outdated policy after the original document changes. The team assumes continued pre-training should remove the need to retrieve current evidence.
meaning: Domain adaptation changes eligible model behavior using suitable text; it is not a real-time source lookup.
evidence: Compare the source/version and context supplied for this request. Evaluate the adapted model against the original baseline on representative held-out tasks.
rule: Continued pre-training is model-specific and does not replace current evidence retrieval.

title: The cheaper student loses a critical task
situation: A smaller distilled student reduces serving cost but fails a critical cohort that the teacher handled correctly. Average quality remains acceptable.
meaning: Lower cost is useful only when the student preserves the required task quality, including critical cohorts.
evidence: Compare teacher/student outputs on the same held-out tasks; inspect cohort quality, safety, latency, and cost before promotion.
rule: Do not promote an average improvement that violates a critical requirement. Distillation differs from quantization or adding an adapter.
